title: Seven years like a few days (Genesis 29:1–20)
hookLine: Jacob works seven years for Rachel and they seem to him but a few days

cards: Another well. Jacob walks on, to the land of the east, and comes to one in a field. Genesis loves a well: Hagar's, Rebekah's, Isaac's.

Shepherds lie around with their flocks, and a huge stone covers the mouth of the well. They only roll it off when every shepherd has arrived, all together. Then Rachel comes, Laban's daughter, with her father's sheep.
She's a shepherd. And Jacob, the quiet tent-dweller, rolls the great stone off by himself and waters her whole flock. Then he kisses her, lifts up his voice, and weeps.
After the running, the stone pillow, the long road, he has found his mother's family. And he has found her.

teach.b: Laban, Rachel's father, takes Jacob in. After a month of Jacob working for nothing, Laban says: you shouldn't serve me for free. Name your wages.
Now the two daughters. Leah, the elder, whose eyes, the Torah says, were tender, or weak: the Hebrew word can mean either, and readers disagree. And Rachel, beautiful in form and face.
Jacob loves Rachel, so he names his price: I'll serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter. No silver, no bride-price, just work.
Then the verse, in the old JPS translation: "And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her." That's strange.

When you love someone and you're waiting for them, don't days feel longer, not shorter? Anyone who has waited for a wedding, a baby, a soldier's return knows that. Commentators have wrestled with this.
One answer: the love wasn't impatience. Jacob wasn't counting down, wishing the years away. He loved her so much that seven years of work seemed a small price, a few days' worth.
The work itself became part of the love.
Another reading hears it in hindsight: looking back, the years folded up like days. Either way, the verse makes a simple point: time is measured by the heart as well as the clock.
And Jacob, who took a blessing by a trick, now earns a bride by years of honest work. Hold on to that. Tomorrow, the story turns.

how: Jews read Jacob's meeting with Rachel in the Torah portion Vayetze, and the verse about seven years seeming a few days is sometimes quoted in wedding speeches.

practice: Think of one task today you'd usually do while checking the clock: cooking dinner, a long drive to pick someone up, helping with homework, caring for a parent.
Picture the person it's for, let the task become something you give them, not something you get through, and notice if the time feels different. If you pray, you can offer the task as your prayer.
